catalog_quote: Ehret 1980 (snippets, Google's spacing around hyphens normalised): "East Rift languages are less well known, but the noun-in-isolation patterns of Kw'adza are entirely predictable and remarkably similar to those of West Rift tongues. In three-syllable words Kw'adza shows the tone pattern high-low-low, where Iraqw would have high-falling-low, but elsewhere it tends to show patterns identical with those of the West Rift group. The disappearance of significant lexical tone must thus have taken place in the proto-Rift language." new_statements.rule_in_words: Ehret describes Kw'adza as having no lexical tone: the word's pitch pattern is fully predictable, and in three-syllable words it is high on the first syllable and low on the rest (H-L-L); for other word lengths he says only that the patterns are identical with those of West Rift (Iraqw etc.), which the snippet does not spell out. Read as a fixed initial pitch prominence for trisyllables, i.e. a predictable (accentual) system rather than tone. Independently, Claus 1910: 491 marks a 'dynamischer Akzent' (dynamic stress) in his 1908 wordlist; in his suffixed nouns the mark sits variably on the antepenult (búliko, ságiko, múnako, áfuko) or the penult (izegúko, itumbáko, kipunditúko) -- a wordlist observation, not a stated rule.
new_statements.exceptions: Only the Kw'adza/Iraqw difference in trisyllables (Kw'adza H-L-L vs Iraqw H-falling-L); patterns for other syllable counts are said to match West Rift without being given in the snippet.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level tone/pitch patterns in citation forms from Ehret's 1973-74 collections from the last speakers (rememberers); Ehret frames the system as predictable 'tone', not stress; Claus's accent marks come from a single rememberer in 1908.
new_statements.identity_note: Kw'adza (Ehret's spelling, the autonym) = Qwadza (Kruijsdijk, Blažek) = Ng'omvia (Gogo exonym) = Wangómwia / Kingómwia (Claus 1910): one language, kwad1248 / ISO wka. Ehret's 1973-74 data come from the last speakers in Mbulu District; Claus's 1908 wordlist comes from a single rememberer (Kitúnda) of a Gogo-speaking clan in Useria, Ugogo. Extinct since ca. 1976-99; all data are from rememberers.

sources.note: p. 491 'Linguistisches' transcription key: "' = dynamischer Akzent"; the ca. 90-word list on pp. 492-493 (from one rememberer, Kitúnda, 1908) marks the accent on every word, e.g. búliko 'Bett', ságiko 'Kopf', múnako 'Herz', áfuko 'Mund', hiráku 'Mensch' vs izegúko 'Zahn', itumbáko 'Tabak', kipunditúko 'Pfeife', makombitájo 'Huhn' -- position varies between antepenult and penult of suffixed nouns (my observation; no rule stated). Meinhof's remarks (pp. 494-497) discuss cognates, laterals, clicks and numerals only; nothing on accent.
